title: Response times: the 0.1 s / 1 s / 10 s limits

pins.note: 0.1 s: feels instantaneous, just show the result
1 s: flow of thought survives, feeling of direct control lost
10 s: attention limit, needs progress and expected finish

insight: Three perceptual budgets (source 1993) still frame every latency target; past 10 s users need percent-done and a way out.
gitgud: Claude's pick: budget every action into one of the three bands; fetch/LFS pull get progress plus Cancel.

title: Doherty threshold: interact under 400 ms

pins.note: Productivity rises when neither side waits; <400 ms
Takeaway: feedback within 400 ms; perceived performance counts

insight: IBM's 1982 finding sets a looser outer bound than 100 ms; perceived speed (progress, animation) also counts.
gitgud: Claude's pick: 400 ms is the hard ceiling for anything non-network; aim for 50 ms like Superhuman.

title: Applying the 100 ms rule to email

pins.note: Speed as the product's headline promise (2022)
Every interaction under 100 ms; internal target <50 ms

insight: Superhuman treats 100 ms as a ceiling, buckets events into <50/<100/<1000 ms, keeps a local DB and prerenders likely next views.
gitgud: Claude's pick: steal the bucketed latency metric and prefetch the diff of the next commit in the list.

title: GPUI: rendering UI at 120 FPS

pins.note: 8.33 ms per frame at 120 Hz: state, layout, paint
Atom/Electron: GC pause or relayout = missed frame
Built own GPU UI framework to hit the budget

insight: Frame budget, not average speed, is what makes an app feel solid; web stacks lose frames to GC and DOM layout (source 2023).
gitgud: Claude's pick: gitgud runs in WebView2, so draw the graph on canvas from Rust-precomputed lanes and virtualize every list.

title: Searchable keyboard shortcut help on ?

pins.note: Shortcut sheet is itself searchable
Cmd/Ctrl+K opens the command menu
? opens help from anywhere

insight: Linear pairs a command menu that runs any action with a searchable shortcut sheet to convert mouse users to keys (source 2021).
gitgud: Claude's pick: Ctrl+K palette showing each command's shortcut, plus ? for a searchable keymap generated from the same keymap file.

title: 2024 redesign: less noise, more density and hierarchy

pins.note: March 2024 redesign write-up
Goal: reduce noise, increase hierarchy and density
Sidebar, list and detail panels tightened

insight: Linear got denser by removing chrome, and generates every theme from base, accent and contrast in LCH.
gitgud: Claude's pick: few theme tokens in OKLCH with a contrast knob; hierarchy from type and contrast instead of borders.

title: Windows content layout and spacing ramp

pins.note: 8 epx between related controls
12 epx between content areas
16 epx surface-to-edge text

insight: Windows groups UI by a small fixed spacing ramp; WinUI also offers a Compact density for pointer-driven, information-rich apps.
gitgud: Claude's pick: 4 px grid with the 8/12/16 ramp at Compact density, so gitgud feels at home on Windows while staying dense.

title: Undo anything with Ctrl+Z

pins.note: Undo as a headline feature
Standard Ctrl+Z, no special mode
Covers delete, stage/unstage, discard chunk

insight: Tower maps the OS undo shortcut onto git: staging, discards, commits, branch ops, merges, interactive rebases and stashes.
gitgud: Claude's pick: same Ctrl+Z contract, backed by an op log so it survives restarts and covers discards.

title: Operations history: snapshot before every action

pins.note: Snapshots branch state, uncommitted work, conflicts into git ODB
Each entry names the operation and time
Even DiscardChanges is listed, so discards are recoverable
Revert restores state to just before that op

insight: GitButler's oplog covers what reflog misses (working tree, conflict state) by snapshotting before each major action.
gitgud: Claude's pick: same model in gitgud-core under a private ref; the list is the visible undo history.

title: Operation log: undo, revert, restore

pins.note: Every op stores a view: refs, heads, working-copy commit
undo last, revert any op, restore whole repo
--at-op: inspect the repo as it was

insight: jj makes the operation, not the commit, the unit of undo; any past state is viewable and restorable.
gitgud: Claude's pick: offer 'view repo at this op' (read-only graph) before restoring, which fixes the fear in P3.

title: Commit editing by drag and drop

pins.note: Replaces rebase -i: most edits are drag-and-drop
Squash, split, move, undo commits
Commit editor inline in the branch lane

insight: GitButler turns squash, reorder, amend-into and split into drags on the commit list, no rebase todo file.
gitgud: Claude's pick: steal the drags, add a hover preview of the result and a keyboard twin for each.

title: Vision and design principles

pins.note: Seven principles; safety and simplicity win conflicts
'YOU ARE HERE' marker while rebasing
Toast only when the affected entity is off-screen
Disabled keybinding explains why

insight: lazygit codifies discoverability, safety and speed: disable rather than hide, confirm only hard-to-reverse actions, respect git config.
gitgud: Claude's pick: adopt its tie-break (safety and simplicity first, power via palette and keys) as gitgud's own.

title: Confirmation dialogs: only when not overused

pins.note: Overused warnings get clicked through
Good: dialog names the exact file and its details
Weak: '2 items', generic Yes/No

insight: Confirm only serious, irreversible actions; restate the target; label buttons by outcome; prefer undo where possible.
gitgud: Claude's pick: confirm only force-push and remote deletes, naming branch, remote and commits lost.
